newsitem.title: USA: Phelps Dodge faces showdown with Apaches.
newsitem.headline: Phelps Dodge faces showdown with Apaches.

text.p: Phelps Dodge has five months to stop using an Apache Indian reservation to transport water to its huge Morenci copper complex in Arizona, or else the flow will be turned off, a representative for the tribe said.
"The tribe is not interested in having Phelps as guests on the reservation," Bill Byler, the Apache's representative said. "They have been bad neighbours."
Phelps said the Apaches lacked powers to carry out the threat.

The dispute over water transportation is a long-standing bone of contention between Phelps Dodge and the San Carlos Apache Indian Reservation, an area covering 2 million acres east of Phoenix, close to the New Mexico border.
Since 1944 Phelps has been using reservation rivers and pump station to move water from the Black River and the Upper Eagle Creek wellfield to Morenci for just $240 a year, Byler said.
If Phelps is not off the reservation by July 23, it will be thrown off, Byler said.
"The reservation has a police force and they will go out there to apprehend the operators of the pump station and escort them to the boundaries of the reservation," Byler said.
Much of the water flow would then be turned off. Water from the Upper Eagle Creek wellfield which is away from San Carlos, could also be diverted before it reached Morenci, Byler added.
Timothy Snider, Phelps' vice president of Arizona operations, said the Apaches would not be able to evict the company.

"They clearly do not have the right to remove us from the reservation. Only the Secretary of the Interior has the right to do that. This was a right of way granted by the Federal Government," Snider said.
The Apaches say they are worried about wildlife and environmental issues linked to water flows.
Morenci employs some 2,500 people and is the largest copper producing operation in North America, producing close to half a million tons of the metal each year.

Thomas Foster, Phelps' vice president and controller, said the company was investigating alternative water supplies. "Although it would be problematic if we had to cease using this, we would probably get through it," Foster said.
Phelps said the water dispute was part of a broader legislatively authorised comprehensive agreement being negotiated with San Carlos and several Arizona cities such as Scottsdale and Phoenix.
"All parties involved in this have to come to agreement," Snider said.
Byler said any existing agreement regarding water rights have expired, and the bid to solve the dispute collapsed July 23, 1996.
Phelps was then given a year's "grace period" by the tribe to continue drawing water for $20,000 a month while it made arrangements for alternative supplies.

Byler said the tribe turned down an offer of $18 million from Phelps in January, a package which included a lump sum, annual payments and some money for "past damages" for using the reservation without permission.
Phelps also gets some of its water from farmers on Arizona's Gila River, but the San Carlos tribe has gone to court to claim the rights on this water too, Byler said.
Byler said there was plenty of alternative water supplies Phelps could buy, and Morenci's output would therefore not be affected if water from the reservation was stopped.
"But Phelps has told some people on Capitol Hill they will have to reduce the number of shifts at Morenci," Byler said. Very few people from the Apache tribe worked at Morenci, he added.
